response.answer:
Under the updated 'healthy' nutrient content claim rule (89 FR 106064, codified at 21 CFR 101.65(d)), a food that does not qualify for one of the automatic exemptions (e.g., single-ingredient foods from encouraged food groups, or water/tea/coffee) must meet two main criteria to bear the 'healthy' claim:

1. **Food Group Equivalent (FGE) requirement**: The food must contain a specified amount of at least one food group equivalent from the food groups encouraged by the Dietary Guidelines (vegetables, fruits, whole grains, fat-free or low-fat dairy, lean meat/seafood/eggs/beans/peas/lentils/nuts/seeds). The specific FGE amounts vary by product category (individual food, mixed product, main dish, or meal) as set forth in 21 CFR 101.65(d)(3)(ii)–(v) and the associated tables. (21 CFR 101.65(d)(2)–(3); 89 FR 106064)

2. **Nutrient-to-Limit (NTL) requirement**: The food must not exceed specified limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium, expressed as a percentage of the Daily Value for those nutrients. These limits also vary by product category. (21 CFR 101.65(d)(3)(ii)–(v); 89 FR 106064; see also 90 FR 10592 at passage describing the rule as requiring 'FGEs and specific limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium based on a percentage of the Daily Value for these nutrients')

As summarized in the background section of 90 FR 10592 (Doc. 2025-03118): the rule 'requires that, to bear a claim subject to the rule, individual food products, mixed products, main dishes, and meals must meet FGEs and specific limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium based on a percentage of the Daily Value for these nutrients.'

No, that was not a fair reading in mid-2025, and it is definitively incorrect now.

**What was true in mid-2025:** The January 2025 order revoking FD&C Red No. 3 (90 FR 4628, published 2025-01-16, Doc. 2025-00830) was subject to an automatic administrative stay under 21 U.S.C. 371(e)(2) as of February 18, 2025, triggered by the filing of objections. During that stay, the effective dates of January 15, 2027 (food uses, removal of 21 CFR 74.303) and January 18, 2028 (ingested drugs, removal of 21 CFR 74.1303) were suspended pending FDA's resolution of the objections. However, the order itself was a final binding order — not a proposal — and the stay was a procedural pause, not a substantive reversal. The stay did not change the stated effective dates; it merely suspended their operation temporarily. Saying the removal was 'not final and might never take effect' overstated the legal situation: the order was final on its face, and the stay would end once FDA acted on the objections.

**What is the position now:** FDA published a final document on August 5, 2026 (91 FR 50475, Doc. 2026-15920) that (1) overruled all objections, (2) denied requests for a public hearing, (3) lifted the administrative stay as of August 5, 2026, and (4) confirmed the original effective dates of January 15, 2027 and January 18, 2028. The document states: 'we are ending the administrative stay of the January 2025 order, and under the January 2025 order we are repealing the listing for FD&C Red No. 3 in § 74.303 as a color additive in food and § 74.1303 as a color additive in ingested drugs effective January 15, 2027, and January 18, 2028, respectively' (91 FR 50475). This constitutes 'final action on the objections' under section 701(e)(2) of the FD&C Act.

The revocation is therefore fully confirmed and binding. After January 15, 2027, use of FD&C Red No. 3 in food will render such food adulterated (90 FR 4628). After January 18, 2028, the same applies to ingested drugs. No compliance date is separately stated; the operative deadlines are derived from the effective dates (per 2025-00830).

response.answer: Under 21 CFR 101.65(a)(2), a 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim must be made in accordance with the general requirements for nutrient content claims in § 101.13, with one specific carve-out: § 101.13(h) is excepted when the nutrient content claim is made in accordance with paragraph (d) of § 101.65. Section 101.13(h) is the disclosure requirement that would otherwise mandate a statement such as 'See nutrition information for ___ content' when a food exceeds specified levels of fat, saturated fat, cholesterol, or sodium. This carve-out means that a food bearing the 'healthy' claim under § 101.65(d) is not required to include the § 101.13(h) disclosure statement, even if the food would otherwise trigger it. All other provisions of § 101.13 (e.g., type size requirements in (f), general claim requirements in (b), substitute food provisions in (d), etc.) remain applicable to a 'healthy' claim.

response.answer: Yes, your shelf-stable lentil soup labeled 'healthy' is affected by the updated definition of the term 'healthy' under the final rule published at 89 FR 106064 (Doc. 2024-29957, published 2024-12-27). This rule revises 21 CFR 101.65(d) to establish new food-group-equivalent (FGE) and nutrient-to-limit (NTL) criteria for foods bearing the 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim. Under the new framework, your lentil soup would need to qualify under one of the pathways in § 101.65(d)(3): either as a food comprised solely of qualifying ingredients with no other added ingredients except water (paragraph (d)(3)(i), which lists beans, peas, and lentils among qualifying foods), or as a mixed product meeting the FGE and NTL requirements in paragraph (d)(3)(iii). If your soup contains added ingredients beyond water and the listed foundational foods (e.g., salt, oil, seasonings), it would not qualify under the automatic pathway of (d)(3)(i) and would instead need to meet the FGE and NTL limits (added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium) specified for mixed products. The effective date of the rule is April 28, 2025 (as delayed by 90 FR 10592, Doc. 2025-03118). The compliance date is February 25, 2028, as stated in the final rule (89 FR 106064). Until that compliance date, you may continue to use the 'healthy' claim under the prior criteria, but by February 25, 2028, your product must meet the updated requirements of 21 CFR 101.65(d) or remove the 'healthy' claim.

Your supplier is partially correct in a narrow technical sense but draws the wrong practical conclusion. The Red No. 3 order (Doc. 2025-00830, 90 FR 4628, published 2025-01-16) indeed sets no explicit 'compliance date' — it states only effective dates. However, the absence of a compliance date does not mean there is no hard deadline. Once the effective date arrives, the listing in 21 CFR 74.303 is removed, and any food containing FD&C Red No. 3 becomes adulterated under the FD&C Act. The operative deadline is therefore derived from the effective date: January 15, 2027 for food uses (all provisions except amendatory instruction 4), and January 18, 2028 for ingested drug uses (removal of 21 CFR 74.1303). After January 15, 2027, food products colored with Red No. 3 may not legally be introduced into interstate commerce regardless of when they were manufactured or when inventory was acquired.

Important caveat: An administrative stay under 21 U.S.C. 371(e)(2) was in effect from February 18, 2025 through August 5, 2026 (per source doc 2026-15920). That stay has now expired. A stay suspends a provision without moving any date — there is no day-for-day extension. The January 15, 2027 effective date therefore remains unchanged and binding.

In summary: the order sets no 'compliance date' in the sense used for rules like the 'healthy' nutrient content claim (which has a stated compliance date of February 25, 2028, per 89 FR 106064). But the derived deadline from the effective date functions as a hard cutoff. After January 15, 2027, food containing Red No. 3 is adulterated. Your supplier's conclusion that there is 'no hard deadline' is incorrect.
